subject: chopperMotorbike
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: custom chopper motorbike.
Style: Overwatch.
reasoning:
I'm planning the chopper motorbike build in Overwatch style using the SDK, thinking through the joint hierarchy with a root frame joint and wheel joints since the API requires exactly one root joint even for vehicles.

For the aesthetic, I'm leaning toward bold stylized Overwatch panels with matte navy/orange colors and glowing cyan emissive accents, plus an original emblem decal to avoid any copyright issues. The chopper design will feature classic elements: a long raked fork, peanut tank, ape-hanger bars, exposed V-twin engine with fins, drag pipes, and a fat rear tire, with rough dimensions worked out for a ~2.4m length and proportional wheelbase and wheel radii.

Now I'm plotting out the exact coordinates for the wheels, steering head, and front axle to get the fork rake angle right around 40-43 degrees, and figuring out how to construct the tires as lathed profiles along the correct axis.

For the tires, I'm designing a rounded rectangular profile that creates a torus-like ring without touching the axis, and planning to add tread blocks by painting darker patches at intervals around the angle. For the wheel rims, I'm considering either a lathed disc with cut-out spoke patterns or separate star-shaped spokes built from rotated box pieces.

For the spokes themselves, I'm working out how to place rods radiating from the hub to the rim using a ring of items around the axle, making sure the wheel joint's direction aligns the bone along the axle axis so the ring sits in the correct perpendicular plane.

To avoid ambiguity with bone inheritance, I decide to compute spoke endpoints manually rather than relying on the ring helper — using a loop over angles in the wheel's plane, with explicit bone references for each rod. I'm sketching out the overall bike skeleton structure: a root chassis joint, then a steering head joint angled along the fork direction, building outward from there.

I'm now mapping out the rest of the skeleton: front wheel joint parented to steering, rear wheel joint parented to chassis, and a hinge joint for the kickstand. I decide to skip assigning roles to most joints except the kickstand hinge, since the rig doesn't strictly need them, and I'm thinking through the rest pose for the kickstand given that the bike needs to stand upright on both wheels.

I settle on folding the kickstand back at a moderate angle so it doesn't touch the ground, keeping the pose physically plausible. For the wheels, I compute the lathe radius and sink the tire centers slightly below the exact tangent point to avoid floating above the ground plane, then start sketching a telescoping front fork with twin stanchions flanking the wheel.

Now I'm detailing the fork geometry: computing the direction vector from head to axle, placing chrome upper stanchions and thicker dark lower sliders with a midpoint split, and considering adding gaiter rings for extra mechanical detail.

I'm building helper functions for tube segments and ring bands, then constructing the steering head tube and triple tree crown as an oriented box aligned to the fork direction, followed by the handlebar risers for an ape-hanger style.

Still shaping the bar geometry...

I'm also sketching smaller details: a mirror stalk with a stylized round mirror disc, and a chunky round headlight bucket positioned near the fork top above the head.

Now I'm placing the headlight between the fork tubes, angling it slightly downward with a glowing cyan-white emissive lens, then moving on to building a hardtail chopper frame with a down tube.

Still defining frame geometry... I'm laying out the backbone from the head tube down to the seat and rear axle, chainstays, and struts, sizing the chunky tubes around a V-twin engine cradle, and picking a bold Overwatch-style palette with dark gunmetal frame tubes and orange bodywork accents.

I'm deciding to skip the kit's glow import and instead write a small local glow helper that clones materials and sets emissive values per mesh, avoiding risky external imports while matching the kit's visual effect for textured and solid-color parts alike.

For the custom paint style, I'm going for a painterly Overwatch-like look: smooth gradient shading based on normal direction (warm highlights on top, cooler darker tones below) with a subtle rim light rather than hard toon bands, plus noise-based weathering like dusty mottling near the bottom and wheels, and a racing stripe defined by position thresholds along the x-axis with a thin contrasting edge line.

Now I'm planning the decal textures needed for the bike: an emblem badge on the tank sides, a speedometer gauge face, headlight and tail light lens glows, a chevron stripe decal on the rear fender, and a number plate texture — aiming for roughly 180-300 total parts across all these components.

I'm then sketching the remaining surface details: a license plate with "OVRDRV" text, quilted diamond stitching on the seat using a paint pattern rather than a texture, and a tire sidewall decal with curved "OVERDRIVE" text wrapped around a disc.

For the rest, I'm planning to keep things mostly as flat paint rather than textures — engine fins, rim spokes, and a blued heat gradient along the exhaust pipes. I'm also leaning into a sci-fi hybrid aesthetic with glowing cyan accents: a lit energy ring in the rear wheel hub, a glowing headlight, and underglow strips along the frame to give it that Overwatch-style tech vibe.

Now I'm setting up the geometry constants for wheel radii, axle positions, and headlight placement, then working out the fork length and rake angle to confirm it reads as a proper chopper silhouette. I'm defining the joint hierarchy starting with the chassis bone and figuring out the right default direction and orientation for the root joint.

Continuing to lay out the skeleton—adding steering, front wheel, rear wheel, and kickstand joints, debating whether to include extra grip joints for throttle detail. I'm also puzzling through how childless joints get assigned bone length when parts don't declare an explicit bone, since that mapping seems ambiguous.

To resolve this, I'm defining helper wrapper functions that always pass `bone` explicitly, like a `part` helper and `rod` helper that bind geometry, color, and bone together. Writing more helper functions...

Then I'm planning the wheel builder that constructs a tire using a lathe profile around a center axis, bound to its joint, with a defined half-width and segment count.

28 segments keeps triangle count reasonable for the tires. For the tire paint, I'm working out how to distinguish tread from sidewall by checking the normal's axial component relative to the wheel axis—small axial values mean tread, larger ones mean sidewall.

For the tread pattern I want alternating dark chevron lugs based on angular position, using dark vs light tread colors. For the sidewall I'm computing the radius from the wheel center using the world position to paint a thin accent pinstripe ring near the outer edge, giving each wheel that classic rubber-with-stripe look.

Now I'm figuring out the rim geometry as a lathed profile, designing it like a solid mag-wheel disc with a hub and barrel lip, since lathe revolution can't cut actual spoke holes -- so I'll need separate spoke parts plus a thin rim ring profile for the barrel itself.

I realize the tire's inner bead is a flat cylindrical surface at radius R-0.15, so looking through the hole from the side, the rim disk would actually be visible behind it.

I'm weighing how to construct the rim itself - whether to make it a solid dished disc or leave it spoked, since a solid disc would block any spoke cutouts. I'm sketching an annular hoop shape for the rim's outer edge that stays visible as metal along the sides of the wheel.

Then I'll add an inner groove to the rim, plus six thick spokes running from the hub out to the rim's inner radius, a cylindrical hub with a flange ring and emblem cap, and a thin glowing cyan torus ring around the outer edge.

Adding spoke tapering details, plus a lathed brake rotor disc and caliper on the front wheel, and sizing the hub cylinder along the axle.

Working out the sprocket geometry...

I'll place the belt-drive sprocket at x=0.17 on the left side with 20 alternating-radius teeth for a toothed look, then move on to the rear axle rod and nuts.

For the fender I'm planning a bobbed chopper style, built as a swept box-section arc centered on the rear axle, spanning roughly 120° over the top-rear of the tire to give that classic bobbed coverage.

Setting fender radius slightly larger than tire radius, and shaping its cross-section as a flattened box with width running sideways along the binormal axis, keeping it symmetric around the tire.

I'm planning a painted finish for the fender—orange base, cream center stripe, navy edge trim—plus two thin rolled-lip rods swept along the fender edges for a finished look. Moving on to the taillight now.

I'm positioning a glowing red-orange taillight at the rear end of the fender using the tilt angle to compute its mount point, and placing a license plate nearby—roughly a 0.2×0.1 plane angled and facing backward at the fender's trailing edge.

Now I'm figuring out the seat placement: since the rear fender top sits around 0.8 given the oversized stylized wheel, I'm reasoning that a proper chopper solo seat should sit forward of the rear tire rather than directly above it, closer to a realistic low saddle height.

Working through the z-range, the seat spans roughly from z=-0.05 to z=-0.55, tracking where the fender's front curve tucks under at y≈0.65, with the seat top sloping from about 0.78 down to 0.72 so it clears the fender comfortably. I'm now setting up the loft stations defining the seat's contoured shape along this path.

For the seat finish, I'm going with dark leather and orange piping with quilted stitching detail. For the springer suspension look, I'm generating a coil spring using a helix/spiral function, defining the center, starting radius, axis, number of turns, and pitch to create a realistic vertical coil beneath the seat.

Now I'm sketching the fuel tank as a stylized teardrop shape, lofting a series of stations along the backbone with varying widths and heights to taper from a rounded front bulge down to a narrower tail.

I'm checking for collisions against the head and fork tubes: the tank top edges press into the triple tree and upper fork area, so I'm shifting the tank back and lowering its center slightly to clear the handlebar and fork geometry while keeping its width comfortably inside the fork tube spacing.

For the loft sections, I'm deciding on a faceted low-poly style with around 10-12 sides for the tank rather than a smooth circular cross-section. For the paint, I'm defining a toon-shaded function that blends orange, cream, and navy tones based on position and surface normal to create the tank's stripe and outline effect.

Writing shading function...

Still defining the palette...

Placing the crankcase box behind center, then angling the V-cylinders outward from a shared crank point, computing direction vectors for the front and rear cylinders tilted 30° apart.

I notice the rear cylinder top collides with the backbone and tank underside, so I'm shortening the cylinder length and lowering the start point to clear that intersection, recalculating the new top position.

Now I'm moving the crank center slightly lower for ground clearance, then laying out the exhaust as two drag pipes running along the right side from each cylinder's exhaust port back to staggered tail positions.

Still placing exhaust pipe coordinates...

For the heat shield, I'm planning to add perforated clamp-like bands as cylinder discs swept along the pipe path, using an "along" helper that orients each piece to face the tangent direction of the path.

To make sure each ring attaches to the right bone despite the path not carrying one by default, I'll pass the bone explicitly rather than relying on nearest-joint inference.

For the flare tip, I'm shaping the sweep radius to widen near the end, adding a dark glowing disc cap facing backward to suggest depth, then setting up a gradient paint that shifts toward blue heat near the head based on distance along the pipe's z-axis.

Now I'm planning the primary drive side: a lathed round cover near x=+0.16 with chrome, an orange ring accent, and an emblem cap, positioned to match the crankcase width, while the opposite side gets a big round air filter housing in an S&S style.

I'm trying to position this air cleaner between the V-twin cylinders without overlapping the exhaust pipe or cylinder fronts, working out the exact coordinates based on the V angle and cylinder heights to find a clean spot around y=0.6.

Plotting the second exhaust pipe route from the rear cylinder head, checking that it doesn't collide with the first pipe's path through similar coordinate space.

Working out the pipe routing so pipe1 dips down before pipe2 even begins its descent at the rear, avoiding any crossing. I'm mapping pipe2's path as it rises slightly toward the tail, checking whether that tail position lines up near the fender location around x ±0.15.

I'm also checking whether pipe1's route clears the forward-control footpegs and front wheel — the pipe passes behind the pegs at z 0.12 versus the pegs at z 0.40, so no collision, and both pipes clear the front tire's z position comfortably.

Now I'm tracing the front downtube from the head to the engine mount and checking it against the front cylinder and exhaust port — the tube's z-coordinate near y=0.7 stays about 0.09 clear of the cylinder front face, though it comes close to overlapping with where pipe 1 starts near the exhaust port.

I'm rethinking the frame as a single centered backbone tube curving from the head, under the tank, down past the engine, rather than twin downtubes, positioning it around y=0.84-0.95 so the tank sits saddled over it with minimal visible overlap.

I need to check that the rear struts connecting the backbone to the axle plates avoid clipping through the rear tire's circular profile — adjusting the backbone's rear endpoint forward to clear the tire's front edge, then routing the strut paths outward and down to the axle mounts at the tire's width.

I'm checking that fender struts stay clear of the fender edges, then tracing the lower chainstays from the engine rear mount out to the axle, confirming they stay outside the tire's front boundary the whole way.

Now I'm laying out the downtube path from the head down to the bottom cradle, then adding bottom rail rods and chainstays that connect into the axle position, making sure everything clears the tire width.

Checking the bracket rod path against the pipe curve near the peg mount, I confirm there's no collision since they're offset enough in z at that x range.

For the mid-body, I'm considering adding a glowing energy cell cylinder under the seat for a tech vibe, positioning it so it clears the front tire, with a steel housing wrapped around it.

Now I'm designing a chrome sissy bar rising from the rear fender struts behind the seat, checking its curve path stays clear of the rear tire's position.

Now thinking about the front fender, a small bobbed arc over the front tire near the axle, and whether it needs to rotate with the steering since the fork axle sits on the steering axis.

I'm narrowing the fender half-width to about 0.085 so it just clears the fork tubes while staying narrower than the tire, then checking it against the front axle height for ring placement.

Now I'm working through the geometry of how the fork angles back relative to the tire top, computing where the fork tube sits at the same height as the tire's highest point so the fender arc can wrap correctly around that offset.

I also need to add a handlebar clamp rising to about 1.45 units, and place a small gauge/dial housing on the rear of the tank top, angled upward and back with a cylindrical housing and face plane positioned using the surface normal.

Checking the tank's loft profile at different stations to estimate the tank's top height near the gauge location, I'm interpolating between the nearby cross-sections to land on a reasonable center position for the gauge housing, accepting some overshoot from the catmull interpolation.

Better approach: using a ray cast straight down onto the tank surface to find the exact hit point and normal, then seating the gauge housing and face there with proper embedding so it sits flush against the curved surface. I'm planning a helper function that performs this raycast and returns the hit or throws if nothing's found, then orienting the gauge face circle along the hit normal, possibly blending in a slight tilt toward the rider for readability.

Now I'm thinking through the emblem decals on the tank sides, using a similar raycast-to-surface approach to find attachment points and outward-facing normals, while being careful about how direction and mirroring work for the left versus right side so the emblem reads correctly from the viewer's perspective.

I'm skipping the racing number idea and instead designing the headlight: a lathed bucket shape with a chrome ring and glowing lens, oriented along the fork's forward direction, then positioning it between the fork tubes with appropriate offsets.

I'm adjusting dimensions so the headlight bucket doesn't clash with the fork stanchions or front tire—shrinking the headlight radius to 0.08, spacing the forks to ±0.125, and recalculating the fork axis and headlight mounting coordinates relative to the head tube position.

I realize placing the headlight directly on the fork axis causes the bucket's rear to intrude into the steering head tube, so I'm shifting the light center forward along the fork direction plus an offset to clear that conflict, landing on coordinates around (0, 0.935, 0.625) and checking the rear edge of the bucket against the head tube radius.

I'm also checking that the lathe-generated bucket shape doesn't clip into the front tire by comparing its forward extent against the tire's circular profile at that height, confirming there's clearance. Then I'm sketching support rods connecting the fork tubes to the bucket sides, and working out placement for the front brake disc and caliper—shifting the disc to the opposite fork side to avoid overlapping the tire width, sizing it relative to the slider position, and noting the caliper box needs to sit on the slider too.

Now I'm sizing the wheel spokes relative to the rim's inner radius, making sure the brake disc sits behind them and clears the slider and hub extents. I'm also laying out the axle rod with nuts, deciding on a wheel color gradient, and planning the fork details—chrome stanchions, a navy-and-orange slider with accordion boot rings, then the triple tree plates, head tube, top cap, and handlebar riser clamps.

Writing the bar and grip geometry...

Mirror stalks with glossy cyan discs facing backward, then skipping cables for simplicity but adding a couple black loops for detail. I'm skipping extra foot controls and focusing on the drive belt geometry, computing tangent lines between the rear sprocket and a small pulley to approximate the top and bottom belt runs.

Checking positions, I realize the sprocket placement overlaps with the rear strut mounts at x=0.17, so I need to shift the sprocket slightly inward to avoid the collision while keeping clearance with the tire width.

Checking the chainstay-belt clearance confirms different x positions, so no overlap there. The rear sprocket at radius 0.17 sits outside the tire sidewall at x=0.13, so that clears too. Moving on to verify the rear axle rod placement at the hub.

Now I'm thinking through the lathe part specification — the outline needs at least 3 non-self-crossing corner points, the axis direction determines radial vs axial orientation (with x radial and y axial along the given axis), and each lathe part needs a bone assignment. I'm also weighing paint and color budget: aiming for roughly 25 flat colors, keeping paint sheet size at the default 1024 to avoid exceeding atlas limits, and estimating texel density against the bike's ~2.6m length and painted surface area to make sure resolution stays reasonable.

I'm narrowing down which helper functions to import from the builder library, keeping only the ones actually needed to avoid unused-import errors, then starting to define local type aliases and vector helpers for the geometry code.

Setting up color palette constants for orange, navy, cream, and accent tones, then writing paint helper functions that apply toon-style shading by darkening and cooling colors based on surface normals.

Writing chrome paint shader...

Now defining a dark metal toon material for the engine with slate coloring, fine noise texture, and a sheen highlight.

Rubber gets the standard toon treatment, and for the seat I'm working out a quilted leather pattern using diagonal UV coordinates to create diamond stitch lines on the upholstery, applying a brown-black base with orange stitching visible only on upward-facing surfaces.

For the shading I'm adding a subtle puffed-lighten effect near the quilt centers to simulate padding depth. Then I'm moving to the tank paint, planning cream and navy racing stripes along the x-axis plus a darker swoosh gradient toward the lower tank area.

Now I'm defining a jagged two-tone boundary for the tank: orange on top, navy below with a zigzag edge line traced along the z-axis and a thin cream highlight tracing the seam, then moving on to the fender with its own orange base and cream double-stripe with navy edges.

I'm layering in weathering touches: a noise-driven scuff function that darkens lower surfaces subtly, applied lightly to fenders and tank, plus a dusty tan-brown mud mix on the lower portion of the tires using noise for a natural, uneven look. With the surface treatments defined, I'm ready to start building out each piece of geometry.

Setting up the builder structure next — defining the module's metadata and a build function that creates the chopper's joint hierarchy: chassis, steering, front and rear wheel axles, and a kickstand joint with a hinge role, positioning each with specific offsets and directions so the frame geometry can attach correctly. I'm working out the kickstand's folded/tucked orientation now.

Checking overall height stays under control: bars top plus sissy bar gives about 1.46, well within tolerance. For the wheel geometry, the 28-segment polygon means the lowest point dips slightly depending on vertex alignment—either a vertex sits about 0.005 below center or a flat edge sits about 0.0025 above—so I'll just use a small sink value around 0.006 for the ground contact, which stays safely within the 2% tolerance either way.

I'm defining a wheel-building function that takes a joint, center, radius, and half-width, plus options for rear wheel handling, which will use a lathe operation to generate the tire geometry. I'm writing the tire's cross-section profile as a set of points tracing the tread, chamfer, and sidewall curves, with sharper creases preserved at the tread edges and smoother transitions on the sidewall slopes—then figuring out how to detect which faces are tread versus sidewall for painting purposes based on the normal's radial component.

For the sidewall decoration, I'm reasoning through how to add a stripe or ring detail: since the sidewall is curved rather than flat, a simple decal disc won't sit flush against it, so instead I'll rely on paint-based rings (a pinstripe and an orange accent) applied directly along the sidewall curve, plus a separate textured disc for the hub cap emblem.

I'm sketching out a fake "lettering" effect by painting cream-colored blocks in a repeating angular pattern around a ring on the sidewall, then moving on to the rim design: a lathed hoop profile colored gunmetal/navy with chrome spokes and an orange hub cap, plus a thin cyan glow ring added as an annulus on the rim's side face to tie the palette together.

Now I'm working through the spokes: planning 8 chrome rods per wheel that alternate axial direction between hub and rim to create a laced, V-shaped mag-wheel look, scaling the rim's axial depth and spoke endpoints based on whether it's a front or rear wheel, then moving to defining the hub as a cylinder along the axle with radius and length varying between front and rear.

I'm adding navy flange discs at the hub ends, orange cone-shaped center caps with a glowing cyan tip, and simple annular brake discs (steel chrome, perforations skipped for simplicity) positioned near the rear hub. I confirm the tire proportions -- thin front, fat rear chopper-style -- then start writing the fork geometry code, computing a direction vector between fork axle and head points.

Writing fork tube code...

I'll skip explicit fender stay brackets since the fender already sits close enough to the slider tubes to visually read as attached. I'm reconsidering a bridge between the sliders near the fender, but need to check it wouldn't collide with the tire's top profile at that position.

Writing handlebar curve code...

Still working out mirror geometry...

Scaling the mirror to flatten it slightly, then sketching a thin dark throttle cable curve from grip to head. Now I'm starting the chassis frame tubes, defining a navy toon frame color and sweeping the backbone path through a series of points down the bike's spine.

Still writing frame geometry...

I'll skip the engine plate brackets and motor mount rods between backbone and cylinder as redundant detail, and move on to considering bridging struts connecting the rear fender stays to the fender itself.

I'll settle on two fender brackets per side with thin chrome rods, then move on to defining the seat shape using a chassis of bone stations for the loft.

Checking the backbone-seat clearance, I realize the seat center needs to sit higher since the backbone tube would otherwise poke through at z=-0.28 — bumping seat center up to y=0.85 with height 0.1 so it clears the top of the backbone at 0.81.

I'm testing an alternative backbone path that descends more steeply, then recalculating seat heights at each z-station so the saddle stays clear of the frame tube while keeping the rear horn and front rise natural-looking.

Defining seat station widths...

I'm skipping the separate bottom pan since the loft already covers it, and planning an orange piping band swept around the seat at mid-length using a closed loop cut through the seat surface.

Rather than a full circumferential band, I'm considering side piping instead -- sweeping along the seat's lengthwise curve at specific clock angles using a line-based path, assuming the loft object exposes that method similarly to a sweep.

Defining the side piping curve with a catmull path, letting the nearest surface points land correctly on the seat sides, and confirming the surface API takes the loft's return value directly like in the documented example.

For the rear fender, I'm working out the arc sweep geometry: given the center and axis along +X, I verify the rotation direction so a positive angle sweeps the circle point from rear toward front, confirming θ should range from -72° to +53° for a 125° sweep.

I'm now thinking through the fender's cross-section shape -- considering a box versus an octagonal profile with slightly curved sides to give it a crowned, tube-like look, while keeping it thin enough not to appear chunky, and making sure it clears the tire radius underneath.

Now I'm working out the front fender dimensions and angular span, computing the arc's start and end points using a polar helper that converts an axle-centered radius and angle into 3D coordinates, so the fender wraps properly around the front wheel and fork area.

I'm checking fork clearance against the fender: tracing the fork axis height at a given y to find its z-position, then comparing the perpendicular distance to the fender surface to confirm there's no collision, since the fender and slider are offset enough in x to stay separated.

I'm also noting the fender gets an orange body color with a cream stripe, and starting to think about the rear tail light as a glowing red box placed near the fender's rear edge using the same polar positioning approach.

Now I'm working out the taillight housing dimensions and placement, planning a small red-glow lens box with navy housing mounted just below the fender tip, plus a license plate positioned clear of the rear tire with a connecting support rod from the fender to the plate. I'm also sketching the plate's texture as a cream/yellow background with a navy border and stamped text like "OVRDRV" in a monospace font.

Now I'm designing a gauge texture with ticks, a needle, and a glowing cyan arc on a dark face, then moving to an emblem design -- a navy hexagon badge with an orange ring border, a cream lightning bolt shape, and orange wing-slash accents on either side, meant to be applied as a decal on the tank sides and possibly the air cleaner cover.

I'm settling on a final texture set: emblem, gauge, headlight lens, plate, a glowing cyan circuit-trace pattern for the energy cell side panels, and a small hub cap emblem, giving around six to seven reusable decal textures total.

Now I'm placing the circuit decal on flat crankcase side-cover plates flanking the engine rather than directly on the cylindrical cell, with the left cover acting as a primary-drive cover and the right showing the glowing circuit pattern. I'm defining the crankcase itself as a boxy gunmetal block positioned behind the main body, considering whether to add beveled edges for a more mechanical look.

Working out the rocker cover and head positions, checking that coordinates for the rear cylinder head and backbone don't overlap with the tank geometry.

I'll raise the backbone curve further rearward so it clears the rear cylinder head, then adjust the seat height accordingly—settling on a seat around y=.87-.93 with the tank bottom near .835, which checks out against the rear head clearance but runs a bit tall compared to the fender; still workable for this stylized chopper look.

Now I'm reconsidering the springer seat setup: lowering the seat pan to sit around .83-.84 so it reads as suspended on visible coil springs above the fender, with a visible gap between fender and seat bottom. I'm placing those springs symmetrically near the rear stay, rechecking that the backbone curve still passes under the seat without poking through, and confirming the tank tail and seat front overlap is acceptable. The resulting seat height comes out close to .89, which is tall for a rider but fits the proportions given the oversized tires.

I'm sketching helper geometry for the suspension: coil springs built as small spiral sweeps anchored between the rear stay top and the seat underside, plus a generic cylinder-between-two-points helper for things like fins, exhaust flanges, and other angled tube parts, with options for tapering and segment count.

Now I'm checking placement of the exhaust pipes and air cleaner to make sure they don't visually overlap with the crank covers, then defining the air cleaner as a lathed profile along the X axis with a chrome body and an accent-colored center disc.

I'm also checking the energy cell housing beneath the seat against the seat stays, rear cylinder head, and front tire clearance to confirm its position and radius keep it clear of those parts.

Now I'm working out the footpeg brackets, placing rods from the frame out to each peg location with rubber cylinders and chrome end caps, while checking clearance against nearby exhaust pipes.

Then I'm considering underglow accents, deciding to add thin cyan glow strips on the fork sliders rather than along the chassis rails, keeping the lighting subtle rather than overdone.

I'm writing a glow helper that caches modified materials in a WeakMap keyed by material and strength, applying emissive adjustments to mesh materials across sweeps and parts, and confirming it's safe to mutate materials before the export pipeline bakes and merges meshes into the atlas as the kit already does.

For textured elements I'm planning a headlight lens with a radial cream-to-cyan gradient and tinted glow, then sketching out a texture list covering emblem, gauge, lens, plate, and circuit graphics, aiming for roughly six total within the five-to-twelve target. To push part count toward 200+, I'm planning loops for seam rivets and fender mount bolts using small spheres placed along paths, plus fork ribs.

Now I'm adding tank details: a chrome filler cap with a small knob on the left top, a fuel petcock cylinder on the lower side, and a glowing cyan pinstripe swept along a draped path following the tank's side contour on both sides. I'm defining station points along the tank rear to control its shape.

Still writing tank stations...

I'm checking clearances between the headlight, tank front, head tube, and handlebar risers to make sure nothing overlaps, and confirming the loft function's height and width parameters correctly map to vertical and horizontal circle diameters for the tank shape.

Now I'm thinking through the overall stylization — oversized tank, fat tire, chunky fork, ape bars, bright orange and cyan palette for an Overwatch-style readable silhouette — and considering small details like a kickstand foot and front fork brace, skipping a number plate idea.

Writing tire paint function...

Adding dusty tire blending and rim paint details...

Now I'm sketching the wheel function itself, defining a lathe geometry for the tire using radius and axial profile, positioned at the joint's center with the axis running along x.

Writing wheel geometry and spokes...

Adding hub flanges and cone caps...

Defining disc material and sprocket gear tooth outline geometry...

Actually I should shrink the sprocket instead, going with a smaller radius so the glow ring at 0.162 stays visible, then adjust the belt tangent points and rear pulley coordinates to match the new sprocket size.

Now I'm connecting belt rods from the top sprocket points down to the pulley, treating each as a tangent segment, and checking they don't overlap. I'm also placing the pulley as a steel cylinder with a flange near the primary cover, positioning the crankcase separately along z so the pulley and transmission case don't collide, then linking a rod from the crank to tie it all together.

Now I'm placing the transmission box between the crankcase rear and the tire, and resolving a vertical overlap with the engine cell above by shrinking the transmission box height. Then I'm checking the kickstand pivot location, ruling out spots that conflict with the belt or transmission box, and shifting it until it clears those obstacles.

Actually repositioning the pivot forward-out instead so the foot clears the peg properly — that placement works better. I'll make the kickstand a thin steel rod with a small dark box foot, and also add some orange hex HUD-style markers for that Overwatch-inspired detail.

Roughly tallying part counts across the frame, fork, bars, wheels, engine, pipes, tank, seat, fenders, sissy bar, and misc details, I land around 250 total pieces. Now I'm setting up the TypeScript file, importing the builder utilities I'll need and being careful to drop any unused imports so the typecheck doesn't complain. Writing metadata and component code...

Still writing paint helper...

I'm adding a scuff/wear function that blends in a dark tint based on noise and vertical position, plus a dirt tint near the bottom, then building the tank's paint logic to split orange body color from navy/cream stripes using jagged edge noise on the sides and centered stripes on the top face.
